Ten binary result positions encode 2^10 = 1,024 possible patterns, enough for 1,000 bottles. Number bottles 0 through 999 and write each number in ten-bit binary. Tester j receives a sample from every bottle whose bit j is one. The testers' positive/negative pattern is exactly the marked bottle's binary code. For example, bottle 13 has ones at bit positions 0, 2 and 3, so those testers are positive and the others negative. Bottle 0 is sampled by no tester; an all-negative result identifies it under the exactly-one-marked assumption. Nine testers are insufficient because they encode only 512 patterns.

Spoken walkthrough

“I use the testers as binary digits, rather than assigning one tester to one bottle. Ten digits encode 1,024 identities. Each tester samples all bottles with their digit set, and the result pattern decodes the bottle number.”

Trap

If no bottle might be marked, the all-negative pattern becomes ambiguous with bottle 0. If multiple bottles can be marked, the bitwise combination may not identify them uniquely. The exact-one assumption is essential.

Solved similar variant

For 2,000 bottles under the same rules, ten testers are not enough because 1,024 is below 2,000. Eleven testers suffice because 2^11 = 2,048. The minimum is the smallest integer t with 2^t at least the number of possible bottle identities.

Role transfer

For a hypothetical fault-isolation test, encode candidate faults with distinct signatures. Before choosing a test plan, count the information available and check whether the observation model can identify a unique cause.

Q18 — One hundred prisoners share a room with a light switch. How can one safely declare that everyone has visited?

Context and assumptions

The prisoners agree on a strategy in advance. One prisoner is selected each day to visit a room privately; they can inspect and change one persistent on/off switch. The switch starts off. Selection is independent and gives every prisoner a positive probability each day, so everyone is selected repeatedly with probability one. No other communication occurs. The puzzle asks for an eventually correct declaration, not a guaranteed deadline.

Full derivation and answer

Choose one prisoner as the counter. Each of the other 99 prisoners sends exactly one signal in their lifetime: on a visit when the switch is off, turn it on, then remember never to turn it on again. If it is already on, leave it and wait for another opportunity. The counter turns an on switch off and increments a private count. The counter never turns it on. When the count reaches 99, every other prisoner has sent their unique signal, so all have visited; the counter has also visited by definition. No signal is counted twice because only the counter resets the switch and every other prisoner signals at most once. Under the selection assumption, the waiting eventually ends with probability one, although it has no fixed worst-case number of days.

Spoken walkthrough

“I make the switch a one-bit message channel, not a counter. Each non-counter contributes exactly one message. A designated counter consumes each message by turning the switch off. Ninety-nine consumed messages prove that all other prisoners have visited.”

Trap

Do not let everyone turn the switch on repeatedly; the counter could count the same person many times. If the initial switch state is unknown, an initial on state can create a false extra signal, so this specific protocol's proof no longer holds. An unfair scheduler could also withhold a prisoner forever.

Solved similar variant

For five prisoners with a known-off switch and the same selection rule, designate one counter and four one-time signalers. The counter declares at count four. The proof is unchanged: each increment corresponds to a distinct non-counter's visit.

Role transfer

This is a useful analogy for an idempotent distributed event: a producer must contribute one logical effect even if it is scheduled or contacted repeatedly. The protocol also separates correctness from how long completion takes.

Probability and AI-research adaptations

Q19 — Turn an unknown biased coin into an unbiased decision.

Context and assumptions

Repeated tosses are independent with a fixed unknown heads probability p, where 0 < p < 1. The bias must not drift between the two tosses in a pair. A fair output means that the two output labels have equal probability.

Full derivation and answer

Toss twice. Output heads for HT and tails for TH. Discard HH and TT, then start a new pair. HT has probability p(1−p), while TH has probability (1−p)p, so the accepted outcomes have equal probabilities. Conditioning on acceptance gives one-half for each output. A pair is accepted with probability 2p(1−p). The expected number of pairs until acceptance is 1/[2p(1−p)], so expected tosses per output are 1/[p(1−p)]. With p = 0.8, this is 1/0.16 = 6.25 tosses. Correctness does not require knowing p; efficiency depends on it.

Spoken walkthrough

“I use pairs because reversing the order of one head and one tail gives the same probability even for a biased coin. I discard the unequal-probability same-face pairs and map the two balanced mixed pairs to my two outputs.”

Trap

Simply flipping the output label on alternate tosses does not make each individual decision unbiased. The pair method also fails if the two tosses have different biases or relevant dependence.

Solved similar variant

With p = 0.6, pair acceptance is 2 × 0.6 × 0.4 = 0.48. Expected tosses are 2/0.48 = 25/6, approximately 4.167. The accepted output is still exactly balanced under the assumptions.

Role transfer

For a hypothetical AI evaluator, a correction method needs a model of the bias it removes. Proving symmetry under fixed independent draws does not establish robustness to drifting or correlated model judgments.

Q20 — An AI checker flags a rare issue. What fraction of its flags are likely correct?

Context and assumptions

This is synthetic quality screening of generated artifacts, not clinical screening. Suppose 1% of artifacts contain an issue, the checker flags 90% of issue-containing artifacts, and it wrongly flags 5% of clean artifacts. These rates are assumed exact for the exercise. Sensitivity means the issue-detection rate; false-positive rate means the flag rate among clean artifacts.

Full derivation and answer

Use 10,000 artifacts to make the denominators visible. There are 100 issue-containing artifacts; the checker flags 90 and misses 10. There are 9,900 clean artifacts; it wrongly flags 495 and correctly leaves 9,405 unflagged. Among 585 total flags, only 90 are true issues. Therefore P(issue given flag) = 90/585 = 2/13, approximately 15.38%. This is positive predictive value, the fraction of flags that are correct. Bayes' formula gives the same result: (0.90 × 0.01) / [(0.90 × 0.01) + (0.05 × 0.99)]. A high detection rate can coexist with a low fraction of correct alerts when issues are rare.

Spoken walkthrough

“I will turn percentages into counts. In ten thousand artifacts, the checker catches ninety real issues but also flags four hundred ninety-five clean artifacts. So a flag is correct ninety out of five hundred eighty-five times, about 15%.”

Trap

Do not report 90% as the probability that a flagged artifact is bad. That reverses the conditioning. Also distinguish specificity, 95% here, from positive predictive value, about 15.38%.

Solved similar variant

If issues instead occur in 10% of the same 10,000 artifacts with the checker rates unchanged, there are 900 true positives and 450 false positives. Positive predictive value becomes 900/1,350 = 2/3, approximately 66.67%. The checker did not change; the base rate did.

Role transfer

When proposing an agent safety or hallucination checker, estimate the deployment base rate and review load. A balanced benchmark's precision need not transfer to a setting where problematic outputs are much rarer.

Q21 — Model A scores better overall, but Model B scores better on every task type. Is that possible?

Context and assumptions

Consider synthetic binary success counts for easy and hard tasks. A and B were evaluated on different task mixes. The comparison concerns arithmetic; these counts do not establish statistical significance or actual model quality.

Full derivation and answer

On easy tasks, A succeeds on 81 of 90, or 90%, while B succeeds on 10 of 10, or 100%. On hard tasks, A succeeds on 2 of 10, or 20%, while B succeeds on 27 of 90, or 30%. B is better within both task types. Yet A's combined score is (81+2)/(90+10) = 83%, and B's is (10+27)/(10+90) = 37%. A received mostly easy tasks and B mostly hard ones. This reversal is a form of Simpson's paradox: subgroup proportions change the aggregate comparison. With a shared 50% easy, 50% hard task mix, A's standardized rate is 0.5 × 90% + 0.5 × 20% = 55%, while B's is 0.5 × 100% + 0.5 × 30% = 65%.

Spoken walkthrough

“Yes, if the models see different difficulty mixes. In this constructed example B wins within each group, but A's test contains many more easy tasks. I would compare them on the same examples or reweight to an explicitly agreed target mix.”

Trap

Do not average subgroup percentages without specifying the weights, and do not use a changed task mix as evidence of a model improvement. This example also has a small easy-task sample for B, so real research would need uncertainty estimates and stronger evaluation data.

Solved similar variant

For a target workload that is 80% easy and 20% hard, A scores 0.8 × 0.90 + 0.2 × 0.20 = 76%; B scores 0.8 × 1.00 + 0.2 × 0.30 = 86%. B still leads by ten percentage points under shared weights. The target mix changes the absolute scores, but not this within-group advantage.

Role transfer

For a hypothetical agent evaluation, hold the repository, tool difficulty and failure-type mix fixed before comparing versions. Report subgroup counts alongside aggregates so a composition shift cannot masquerade as progress.

Q22 — A tool call succeeds with probability 0.7. With at most three attempts, what are success probability and expected calls?

Context and assumptions

Each attempt independently succeeds with probability p = 0.7. Stop immediately on success. Three attempts means the initial call plus at most two retries. Every attempt costs two fictional credits. Failures are retryable, have no side effects, and do not change later success probability. These are toy assumptions, not measurements of the Sandbox or a provider.

Full derivation and answer

Write q = 1−p = 0.3. All three attempts fail with probability q^3 = 0.027, so eventual success is 1−0.027 = 0.973, or 97.3%. For expected calls, count whether each call is reached. Call 1 is always made, call 2 occurs after one failure with probability 0.3, and call 3 occurs after two failures with probability 0.09. Therefore E[calls] = 1 + 0.3 + 0.09 = 1.39. Expected cost is 2 × 1.39 = 2.78 credits. The full count distribution is P(one call) = 0.7, P(two calls) = 0.21 and P(three calls) = 0.09; the last group includes third-call success and total failure. In general, with K attempts, E[calls] = 1+q+q^2 through q^(K−1) = (1−q^K)/p for p > 0.

Spoken walkthrough

“I compute success by subtracting the all-fail path. For cost I count how often each attempt is reached, rather than multiplying the maximum by the success rate. That gives 97.3% success, 1.39 expected calls and 2.78 expected credits.”

Trap

Three retries usually means four attempts; clarify the contract before calculating. Correlated failures, rate limits, changing prompts and repeated side effects invalidate the simple independent model. A retry policy also needs an idempotency or compensation design when calls can write data.

Solved similar variant

With p = 0.5 and at most four attempts, failure is (1/2)^4 = 1/16. Success is 15/16 = 93.75%. Expected calls are 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 = 15/8 = 1.875. At two credits per attempt, expected cost is 3.75 credits.

Role transfer

When evaluating an agent's retry policy, measure the empirical failure dependence and distinguish the call cap from expected spend. A constant named MAX_RETRIES does not establish either the state semantics or these assumed probabilities.

Q23 — Do two parallel 95%-reliable services make a 99.75%-reliable system?

Context and assumptions

The system succeeds if at least one service is available. First assume each is independently available with probability 0.95 and there is no other failure. Then consider a shared gateway that is down 10% of the time; conditional on the gateway being up, the two services remain independently 95% available. Availability is a synthetic probability for this problem, not an observed service-level agreement.

Full derivation and answer

In the independent-only case, the system fails only when both services fail: 0.05 × 0.05 = 0.0025. Availability is 1−0.0025 = 0.9975, or 99.75%. With the shared gateway, the system can succeed only when the gateway is up, probability 0.9. Conditional on that, at least one service is available with probability 0.9975. Overall availability is therefore 0.9 × 0.9975 = 0.89775, or 89.775%. A single such service behind the same gateway would give 0.9 × 0.95 = 85.5%. Redundancy helps within the dependency boundary, but cannot bypass the shared outage. The two end-to-end service paths are correlated because both depend on the gateway.

Spoken walkthrough

“The 99.75% result needs independent failure and no missing dependency. Once a shared gateway is required, I multiply by its 90% availability. The result is 89.775%, so duplicating the service does not remove the common failure mode.”

Trap

Do not treat two paths as independent merely because they use different model instances. They may share credentials, a rate limiter, a database or a network route. The stated 95% is conditional on the gateway being up, so it must not be confused with end-to-end availability.

Solved similar variant

Two services are each independently 90% available when their common gateway works, and that gateway works 80% of the time. The parallel conditional availability is 1−0.1^2 = 0.99. Overall availability is 0.8 × 0.99 = 0.792, or 79.2%. The 80% shared dependency creates an upper bound that service duplication cannot exceed.

Role transfer

For a hypothetical multi-model fallback, map shared dependencies before claiming a reliability gain. A fallback using the same failed tool endpoint may add latency and cost without restoring task success.

Q24 — Four candidates arrive in random order. With no recall, how can I maximize the chance of selecting the best?

Context and assumptions

Four candidates have distinct quality ranks and arrive in a uniformly random order. I see only relative ranks among candidates already interviewed, must accept or reject immediately, cannot recall a rejected candidate, and want the single best overall. This is a secretary-problem exercise, not a claim about hiring or ZS practice.

Full derivation and answer

A threshold strategy rejects the first r candidates, then accepts the first later candidate better than everyone seen; if none appears, it takes the last candidate. For r at least one, condition on the overall best arriving at position j > r. That occurs with probability 1/4. The strategy chooses it exactly when the best among the first j−1 candidates lies in the rejected sample, probability r/(j−1). Thus success is (r/4) times the sum of 1/(j−1) for j = r+1 through 4. Rejecting one gives (1/4)(1 + 1/2 + 1/3) = 11/24, about 45.83%. Rejecting two gives (2/4)(1/2 + 1/3) = 5/12, about 41.67%. Rejecting three or taking the first immediately gives 1/4. The optimal policy is therefore reject the first, then take the next new record. Backward reasoning supports the threshold form: never choose a candidate already worse than a seen one; whether to accept a new record depends only on its position under the random-order model. Enumerating all 24 rank orders verifies these four success rates.

Spoken walkthrough

“I use an initial sample to establish a benchmark, then accept the next record. For four candidates, sampling one wins in eleven of the twenty-four possible orders, better than sampling two or three. I would state the no-recall and random-order assumptions first.”

Trap

Do not apply a large-sample percentage rule mechanically to four candidates. Also, if quality scores are absolute, orders are not random, or candidates can be recalled, this model's optimal policy need not apply.

Solved similar variant

With five candidates, reject the first two. Its success probability is (2/5)(1/2 + 1/3 + 1/4) = 13/30, about 43.33%. Rejecting one gives 5/12, about 41.67%; rejecting three gives 7/20, or 35%; rejecting four gives 1/5. Enumerating all 120 orders confirms that a two-candidate sample is best among these threshold policies and is the optimal no-recall policy for this model.

Role transfer

For a hypothetical sequential experiment budget, make the decision constraints explicit before choosing a stopping rule. In real model development, previous checkpoints can often be revisited, so the no-recall puzzle is an analogy rather than an automatic deployment strategy.

A sourced older EBI anecdote: clarify geometry first

Q25 — Cut a cake into eight equal parts with three straight cuts. Can you give two approaches?

Context and assumptions

A candidate account last updated in August 2021 mentions a cake puzzle in a ZS EBI/Fit round and a request for two approaches. Its wording refers to three knives; this practice formulation explicitly allows three straight planar cuts. It is an older individual account, not an official question bank or a prediction of this interview. [web: https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/interview-experiences/zs-associates-interview-experience-for-business-technology-solutions-associate-on-campus-2/]

Assume an ideal cylindrical cake of uniform height and density. Equal parts means equal volume, not necessarily identical decorations or frosting. A cut may pass through the cake's full width or height. Ask whether moving and stacking pieces between cuts is allowed; the second approach below requires that permission.

Full derivation and answer

First approach: keep the cake intact between cuts. Make two vertical cuts through the central axis, perpendicular to each other. These create four equal quarter-cylinder wedges. Make the third cut horizontally at half the cake's height. Each quarter is divided into equal upper and lower pieces, giving eight pieces of one-eighth the original volume. The cuts divide three independent spatial directions into two parts each, so 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.

Second approach, only if rearranging and stacking are allowed: make the same two vertical cuts to create four equal quarter-cylinder wedges. Place those wedges in a stack with the same footprint and orientation. Make one vertical cut through the stack along the angle bisector of the aligned wedges. This single plane bisects all four quarter-wedges at once. The result is eight equal one-eighth-cylinder pieces. This is a different arrangement-and-cut procedure, not merely a different order of the first approach's three planes.

Spoken walkthrough

“First I would clarify that this is a three-dimensional cake and that equal means equal volume. Two perpendicular vertical cuts make four equal quarters; a horizontal cut at half-height doubles them to eight. For a second approach, I need permission to rearrange: I stack the four quarters in the same orientation and bisect the whole stack with one vertical cut.”

Trap

Making the horizontal cut first and then the same two vertical cuts is the same geometric construction in a different order; do not present it as an independent second method. If stacking is prohibited and the interviewer demands a distinct construction, say which constraints need clarification rather than inventing one. Three arbitrary cuts do not necessarily make equal volumes.

Solved similar variant

For a flat disk with no stacking or rearrangement, three straight line cuts cannot create eight regions at all. Starting from one region, the first line adds at most one, the second at most two, and the third at most three: maximum regions = 1 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 7. Reaching seven does not itself guarantee equal areas. The three-dimensional cake solution succeeds because a horizontal plane can split all four existing vertical pieces simultaneously.

Role transfer

For a hypothetical research problem, clarify the allowed operations and what “equal” measures before optimizing. A solution valid with rearrangement or a third dimension is not evidence that the original constrained version is solved.

Open-ended practice: business judgment and AI research

These eighteen questions are practice choices for a 45-minute ZS EBI conversation, not a prediction of what will be asked. Research is your stated interview context; this guide does not claim that a public source establishes your exact reporting team. The answers use hypothetical first-person language so you can practise a concrete response without inventing a past client result, disagreement or experiment. Adapt a draft only when you can support the personal details.

Priority A means practise early because the question connects several parts of this role. Priority B means a useful second pass. A hypothesis is a statement you can test; a baseline is a simple comparison; an experiment changes a defined factor; a metric measures a defined outcome. Explain the decision each result would support, rather than listing those words.

Eight drills to do first

DrillQuestionPractise this decisionSuggested spoken target
1Q01: unclear client needTurn an unclear request into a measurable problem.90 seconds
2Q02: AI is not neededProtect business value while keeping the client involved.90 seconds
3Q07: choose the approachDecide among a workflow, agent, retrieval and tuning.2 minutes
4Q08: six-repository evaluationExplain what a small evaluation can support.2 minutes
5Q09: defend the metricKeep 0.9184 separate from 36/39 and state the limit.90 seconds
6Q12: wrong retrieval or generationIsolate which part of the system failed.2 minutes
7Q13: prompt injectionMake a concrete safety decision at a tool boundary.2 minutes
8Q18: research into a reusable componentDefine evidence, ownership and a bounded handover.2 minutes

General consulting and collaboration

Q01 — A client says, “Our teams waste time. Build an AI assistant.” What would you do first?

Context

Priority A. This tests whether you can identify the decision behind an unclear request before choosing technology. Use a document-review team as a hypothetical example, not a claimed ZS engagement.

Clarify and structure

Ask which users lose time, on which task, at what volume, and what a good outcome would be. Separate time spent finding material, reading it and correcting mistakes. Choose one workflow, one owner and one measurable pilot.

Draft answer

I would first ask the client to walk me through one recent task, including the inputs, waiting time and corrections. “Wasted time” could mean slow search, duplicate work or unclear approvals, and those need different fixes. Suppose analysts repeatedly locate evidence inside approved documents. I would test the hypothesis that finding the right passage is the main delay. My baseline would be the current search process, measured on a small set of representative tasks. I would compare a better keyword search with an assistant that returns cited passages. I would measure completed-task time, evidence correctness and the review effort left to the analyst. I would agree success criteria with the workflow owner before the trial. If search is only a small part of the delay, I would change the problem statement before expanding the system.

Probe and answer

Probe: what if the sponsor wants a demo next week? I would offer a narrow demonstration using approved sample documents and a few agreed tasks. I would label simulated steps and exclude sensitive live data. The demonstration would test the task hypothesis; it would not count as evidence of time savings until representative users complete a measured comparison.

Similar question with concrete answer

Question: three stakeholders give three different definitions of success. How do you proceed? I would write their desired outcomes side by side, identify the shared user task and ask the accountable owner to choose the first decision. For example, I would make evidence correctness a release condition and review time an improvement measure. I would record which cost and feature requests are outside the first pilot.

Weak-answer trap

Starting with a model name, an architecture diagram or a promised productivity percentage before understanding the work.

Q02 — The client insists on generative AI, but a simpler system may solve the problem. How would you respond?

Context

Priority A. This tests whether you can challenge a proposed solution respectfully and make the alternative easy to assess. Generative AI means a model creates content, such as a natural-language summary.

Clarify and structure

Confirm the required output and the business constraint. Compare the simplest viable rule or search system with an AI option on the same tasks. Discuss error consequences, maintenance, cost and the next investment decision.

Draft answer

I would acknowledge the outcome the client wants and ask what the AI must do that a simpler system cannot. Suppose the task is routing forms with a few stable fields. I would propose a rules-based baseline because its decisions are easier to inspect and its operating cost is predictable. I would also test a model on the difficult, free-text cases, rather than dismissing AI without evidence. Both options would receive the same examples, including missing fields and unusual language. I would compare correct routing, manual review volume, response time and maintenance effort. If rules meet the target, I would recommend shipping them and reserving AI for a justified exception path. If the model handles valuable cases the rules miss, I would propose a bounded hybrid with review for uncertain outputs. The recommendation would follow the measured benefit and risk.

Probe and answer

Probe: would saying no to AI damage the relationship? I would avoid presenting the decision as a rejection of the sponsor. I would show the same desired outcome, a cheaper path to it and a short comparison that could change my recommendation. The sponsor remains involved in deciding which benefit justifies additional complexity.

Similar question with concrete answer

Question: the competitor advertises an agent, so the client wants one. What do you say? I would ask whether users need variable tool selection or a fixed sequence. For a fixed sequence of extracting fields, checking rules and submitting for approval, I would demonstrate a controlled workflow. I would test an agent only on cases that require choosing different actions, then compare completion and failure rates.

Weak-answer trap

Calling the client wrong, or agreeing to an agent simply because the term is fashionable.

Q03 — You discover that an important deliverable will miss its deadline. What would you do?

Context

Priority A. This tests early risk communication, ownership and the ability to protect an essential outcome. This is a hypothetical response, not a claim about a past missed deadline.

Clarify and structure

Identify the blocking fact, the committed outcome, the latest useful delivery date and the smallest safe scope. Give the owner a recommendation with consequences, rather than a vague warning or an unsupported promise.

Draft answer

I would confirm the blocker quickly and tell the delivery owner as soon as I have a credible impact estimate. Suppose the evaluation data arrives late and prevents a complete model comparison. I would explain what is finished, what depends on that data and which conclusion I cannot yet support. I would offer two concrete options: keep the date with a smaller, clearly qualified comparison, or move the date to complete the agreed evidence. I would recommend the smaller delivery only if it still supports the client's immediate decision and meets essential quality checks. I would identify an owner and a revised checkpoint for the blocked work. I would also document the dependency so the team can prevent the same surprise. I would keep the status factual and avoid treating extra hours as a substitute for missing evidence.

Probe and answer

Probe: what if your estimate is uncertain? I would give a range with its assumptions and identify the next event that will reduce uncertainty, such as receiving a usable data sample. I would update the owner at that checkpoint. A precise-looking date without a dependency check would make planning worse.

Similar question with concrete answer

Question: another team blocks your work and does not respond. What would you do? I would send a specific request naming the missing input, its format and the decision date. I would continue work that does not depend on it and prepare a substitute sample if that is legitimate. If the dependency threatens the commitment, I would escalate through the project owner with the impact and the options, without blaming individuals.

Weak-answer trap

Hiding the delay until the deadline, or promising to finish everything without changing scope, resources or timing.

Q04 — You disagree with a research lead's preferred approach. How would you handle it?

Context

Priority B. This tests evidence-based disagreement and respect for decision ownership. Do not convert this hypothetical answer into an invented personal conflict.

Clarify and structure

Restate the lead's hypothesis fairly. Identify the measurable disagreement and the cheapest experiment that could distinguish the alternatives. Separate reversible experiment choices from high-cost commitments.

Draft answer

I would first ask the lead to explain the assumption behind the preferred approach and restate it to check my understanding. Suppose the lead favors fine-tuning, while I think poor document retrieval causes most errors. I would bring examples showing missing evidence, rather than arguing from preference. I would propose a short test: keep the generator fixed and supply the correct passages, then compare the existing pipeline with improved retrieval. If correct evidence fixes the failures, I would prioritize retrieval. If errors persist despite correct context, I would examine the generation or training approach. I would agree on the measure and stopping point before running the comparison. If the lead chooses a different direction after reviewing the evidence, I would support that decision, record the remaining risk and suggest a checkpoint where new results can trigger reconsideration.

Probe and answer

Probe: what if there is no time for an experiment? I would show the strongest existing examples, estimate the cost of being wrong and recommend the more reversible choice. I would ask the decision owner to accept the unresolved assumption explicitly. For a serious safety or privacy issue, I would seek the relevant review before proceeding.

Similar question with concrete answer

Question: a senior colleague dismisses your result. How do you respond? I would ask whether the concern is data quality, experimental setup or relevance to the business decision. I would reproduce one disputed example with the settings and evidence visible. If my experiment is flawed, I would correct it; if the result holds, I would propose a bounded follow-up that addresses the colleague's specific objection.

Weak-answer trap

Claiming that confidence, seniority or a single attractive example settles the disagreement.

Q05 — A promising experiment shows no improvement. How would you explain that result?

Context

Priority A. This tests whether a negative result changes your decision, rather than leading to selective reporting. An ablation removes one component to measure its contribution.

Clarify and structure

Check that the comparison was valid before interpreting it. Report the hypothesis, observed result, uncertainty, relevant slices and the next decision. Separate “not detected here” from “cannot work.”

Draft answer

I would first check whether the experiment actually tested the hypothesis: the same data split, a comparable baseline and no accidental change in preprocessing. Suppose adding a second reasoning step does not improve supported answers but increases response time. I would report both outcomes and show the error categories, not just the average score. If a small subgroup improves, I would check its size and whether I selected it after seeing the result. I would avoid claiming that the extra step never works. My recommendation would be to keep the simpler system for this task unless a targeted follow-up has a clear value. I would preserve the configuration and failed examples so the team can reuse the finding. A negative result is useful when it prevents an unsupported complexity increase and identifies which assumption to test next.

Probe and answer

Probe: what if the result contradicts your own proposal? I would say that the evidence did not support my proposal under the tested conditions. I would check the setup once, then change the recommendation if it is valid. Repeating configurations until one looks favorable would waste resources and distort the conclusion.

Similar question with concrete answer

Question: the experiment improves accuracy slightly but doubles latency. What would you recommend? I would identify which errors were fixed and whether users value that improvement. If the additional correctness matters only for difficult cases, I would test a selective fallback. If the gain is small and does not change accepted task outcomes, I would retain the faster baseline and record the trade-off.

Weak-answer trap

Hiding failed runs, reporting only a favorable slice, or treating an inconclusive small experiment as proof of no effect.

Q06 — How would you balance quality against a deadline for an AI prototype?

Context

Priority A. This tests whether you can reduce scope while retaining meaningful evidence and essential safeguards. Prototype quality depends on the decision it is meant to support.

Clarify and structure

Name the decision, users and consequences of error. Set a minimum evidence and safety boundary. Reduce optional functionality before removing controls that make the result trustworthy.

Draft answer

I would separate what is necessary to support the decision from what would make the prototype more polished. Suppose the team must decide whether a document assistant deserves a larger trial. I would keep a representative task sample, evidence checks, clear limitations and a reproducible evaluation. I would reduce the number of document types, the interface work and optional integrations before removing those checks. I would also distinguish a supervised demonstration from a tool users can rely on for real work. If we cannot establish acceptable evidence support or protect the approved data, I would narrow the demonstration further or recommend delaying that decision. I would explain the trade-off early: what the deadline version can show, what remains unknown and what work is needed next. Delivering on time is useful only when the result is interpreted correctly.

Probe and answer

Probe: which tests would you keep first? I would keep checks tied to high-consequence failure modes and the core claimed behavior: evidence support, authorization boundaries, invalid inputs and the end-to-end task. I would add regression examples for previously observed failures. Cosmetic behavior would receive less attention than a claim or tool action users might trust incorrectly.

Similar question with concrete answer

Question: would you ship with a known defect? I would describe the defect's reach, consequence and detectability. A display issue in a supervised internal demonstration may be acceptable with a clear workaround. A defect that bypasses a tool permission check or silently changes evidence would block that use. I would record the owner and repair condition rather than hiding it in a general disclaimer.

Weak-answer trap

Saying “quality always comes first” without a scope decision, or calling every prototype defect acceptable because it is a prototype.

AI research, evaluation and delivery

Q07 — When would you choose a workflow, an agent, retrieval or fine-tuning?

Context

Priority A. A workflow follows planned steps. An agent can choose actions from observations. Retrieval supplies relevant external evidence; fine-tuning changes model weights. These choices can coexist, but each needs a reason.

Clarify and structure

Ask whether the task needs current knowledge, a stable response pattern, variable action choices or all three. Start with the least complex method that could meet the target, then identify the failure that justifies adding a component.

Draft answer

I would choose the approach from the source of difficulty. If the steps are stable, I would start with a workflow because it is easier to test and bound. If the system must choose tools or change its next action after observing results, I would test a bounded agent against that workflow. If the missing ingredient is current or private information, I would retrieve approved evidence and require citations. If the model still fails a stable behavior despite adequate context and prompting, I would consider fine-tuning using suitable labeled examples. For a repository-to-resume task, I would first preserve evidence locations and use deterministic checks around generation. I would compare supported outputs, successful task completion, latency and cost on the same cases. I would add complexity only when its improvement addresses a measured failure and survives the operating constraints.

Probe and answer

Probe: does using LangGraph automatically make a system agentic? No. A graph can encode a fixed workflow or an adaptive loop. I would point to the actual decision and routing behavior. Resume Builder's current v2 graph has thirteen registered nodes, while its browser path traverses nine and stops at document construction. That node count alone does not establish autonomous planning. [repo: resume-builder-agent/v2/src/rba/graph.py] [repo: resume-builder-agent/v2/src/rba/resume/pipeline.py]

Similar question with concrete answer

Question: why not fine-tune to remember a changing document collection? I would use retrieval first because documents can change without retraining and answers can cite the selected evidence. I would test indexing quality and answer support. I would consider fine-tuning separately for a stable output behavior, while keeping changeable facts in the retrieval layer and evaluating whether the added training improves that behavior.

Weak-answer trap

Calling every multi-step pipeline an autonomous agent, or treating retrieval and fine-tuning as interchangeable ways to guarantee factuality.

Q08 — Your saved evaluation uses six repositories. How would you assess whether the system generalizes?

Context

Priority A. The saved Resume Builder evaluation covers six repositories. It can reveal failures in that sample, but it is not a broad reliability guarantee. A held-out set contains examples excluded from tuning. [repo: resume-builder-agent/v1/evals/results/latest.json]

Clarify and structure

Identify the target repository population and the decision the evaluation supports. Separate development examples from an untouched evaluation set. Design slices around plausible failures, and report counts as well as averages.

Draft answer

I would describe the six-repository result as a small saved evaluation, then define where the system is expected to work. Repository size, language, documentation quality and the presence of misleading claims could all change performance. I would create a development set for fixing prompts and checks, and a separate held-out set for the final comparison. I would include empty or sparse repositories, conflicting documentation, unsupported numbers and source text that attempts to redirect the model. I would compare a conservative evidence-copying baseline with the proposed pipeline. I would report supported-claim quality, missed useful claims, abstentions, cost and failure counts by slice. With a small sample, I would show individual failures and uncertainty rather than imply precise population accuracy. The next investment would follow whether the system improves useful supported output beyond the baseline.

Probe and answer

Probe: what if you cannot collect a large test set? I would combine a small representative set with targeted challenge cases and keep their results separate. Challenge cases test specific weaknesses; they do not estimate how often those weaknesses occur in normal use. I would use the first limited pilot to gather reviewed examples under an explicit data and consent policy.

Similar question with concrete answer

Question: can you report a confidence interval from six repositories? I would be cautious about the unit of independence. Many claims from one repository share evidence and are correlated. I would report the repository-level scores and sample size, then explain what a repository-level resampling analysis assumes. I would not treat every generated statement as an independent sample to make the interval look narrow.

Weak-answer trap

Calling the saved result representative merely because it contains multiple claims, or tuning repeatedly on the same six repositories and calling them held out.

Q09 — What does 0.9184 faithfulness mean, and how is it different from 36 verified claims out of 39?

Context

Priority A. This is a direct evidence probe. The saved value is the six-repository macro mean of whole-summary judge faithfulness. Macro mean weights each repository equally. Structured-claim counts use a separate verification process. [repo: resume-builder-agent/v1/evals/results/latest.json] [repo: resume-builder-agent/v1/evals/judge.py]

Clarify and structure

State the unit, numerator or aggregation rule, dataset and evaluation method before interpreting the number. Keep whole-summary judgments, structured claims and numeric-presence checks separate.

Draft answer

I would say that 0.9184 is a saved macro mean of whole-summary faithfulness across six repositories, rounded to 0.92 on the resume. It is not the fraction of verified structured claims. The saved results separately record thirty-nine generated structured claims, of which thirty-six were marked verified. Those quantities answer different questions and use different units. I would also qualify the saved numeric precision of 1.00: the evaluation checked whether detected numbers appeared as substrings in evidence, which does not prove correct meaning or attribution. A number can occur in a file while the generated claim attaches it to the wrong entity. I would present these as limited evaluation signals, not a universal accuracy guarantee. My next step would be a claim-level, human-reviewed comparison with explicit evidence entailment and an untouched test set.

Probe and answer

Probe: why can the macro mean differ from a pooled statement ratio? Repositories can contain different numbers of judged statements. Averaging each repository's score gives a small repository the same weight as a large one. Pooling all supported statements gives larger repositories more weight. I would identify which question the aggregation should answer and report both with clear labels when useful.

Similar question with concrete answer

Question: a stakeholder says “0.92 means only eight percent of resumes are wrong.” How do you respond? I would correct the interpretation immediately: this score does not measure the fraction of entirely correct resumes. It summarizes evidence support under a particular judge on six repositories. I would show one output with an unsupported statement and explain why document-level acceptance needs its own definition and evaluation.

Weak-answer trap

Computing 36/39 and calling it 0.9184, or describing numeric substring presence as semantic correctness.

Q10 — A human reviewer and an LLM judge disagree. Which would you trust?

Context

Priority A. An LLM judge is a model that scores another output against a rubric. Neither a model score nor one human opinion is automatically correct. The disagreement is evidence to inspect. [repo: resume-builder-agent/v1/evals/judge.py]

Clarify and structure

Separate ambiguous criteria from missing evidence and actual scoring error. Use the same evidence and rubric, inspect the disputed claim, then decide whether the label or the evaluation method needs correction.

Draft answer

I would inspect the disputed example rather than choose a winner by default. I would give the reviewer and judge the same claim, evidence span and definition of support. Suppose the evidence lists a cache, but the claim says it reduced latency by twenty percent. I would mark that claim unsupported unless the evidence establishes the measured improvement, even if the judge accepts it. For an ambiguous claim, I would ask a second reviewer to label it independently and record the reason for disagreement. I would revise the rubric if it mixes factual support with writing quality. I would then measure judge agreement with the adjudicated labels on a separate sample, especially for high-consequence errors. I would keep human review for important uncertain cases until the judge is calibrated well enough for the intended use.

Probe and answer

Probe: what if experts disagree too? I would identify whether the source is incomplete or the wording allows multiple interpretations. Some cases should remain uncertain rather than receive a forced label. I would record an adjudication rule and revise the claim or evidence request if possible. The system can abstain when support cannot be established.

Similar question with concrete answer

Question: two model judges agree. Is that enough? I would check whether they share the same model family, prompt or blind spot. Agreement does not prove truth. I would test both against independently reviewed supported and unsupported examples, including deliberately misleading numbers, and report where consensus still accepts errors before using it to reduce human review.

Weak-answer trap

Treating an expert's title, a judge's confidence or agreement between models as a substitute for evidence and a clear rubric.

Q11 — How would you reduce hallucinations without making the assistant uselessly cautious?

Context

Priority A. Hallucination means unsupported or false generated content. Abstention means declining to make a claim when support is inadequate. Both supported usefulness and error risk matter. Resume Builder's verifier offers mechanical checks with semantic limits. [repo: resume-builder-agent/v2/src/rba/nodes/verify.py]

Clarify and structure

Define which claims require evidence and what the assistant may do when evidence is missing. Measure unsupported outputs together with useful supported outputs and unnecessary abstentions.

Draft answer

I would first define what a supported answer means for the task. For evidence-linked resume claims, I would require a specific source location and check that it supports the claim's meaning, including the subject, quantity and scope. I would use deterministic checks for required fields and exact constraints, then evaluate semantic support separately. When evidence is missing, I would let the system ask a focused question, omit the unsupported detail or state the limitation. I would compare this with a conservative baseline on representative examples. I would measure accepted supported claims, unsupported claims that slip through and useful claims rejected unnecessarily. That prevents a system from looking safe by refusing everything. I would prioritize severe errors, such as invented personal impact, and tune the acceptance policy according to the cost of those errors and the review process.

Probe and answer

Probe: would lower temperature solve it? Lower temperature changes sampling behavior; it does not supply missing evidence or ensure the chosen output is true. I would test it as one setting under the same evaluation, but keep evidence constraints and review. A consistently repeated unsupported claim is still unsupported.

Similar question with concrete answer

Question: your stricter verifier rejects many good claims. What do you do? I would review a sample of rejected claims and separate genuinely unsupported ones from failures of evidence extraction or overly narrow rules. I would improve source selection or claim wording before loosening the acceptance condition. Any change would be tested against known unsupported examples so improved coverage does not quietly increase false acceptance.

Weak-answer trap

Promising zero hallucinations, equating a valid schema with a true answer, or improving a support score by removing almost all useful output.

Q12 — In a retrieval-based assistant, how would you tell whether retrieval or generation caused a wrong answer?

Context

Priority A. Retrieval selects evidence; generation creates an answer from the supplied context. A failure can occur in either stage. This is a proposed diagnostic method, not a claim that VisionDev implements a conventional retrieval-augmented text assistant.

Clarify and structure

Check whether the necessary fact exists in the approved corpus, whether it appears in retrieved passages and whether the generator uses it correctly. Then run a controlled comparison with correct evidence supplied.

Draft answer

I would trace one wrong answer through the evidence path. First, I would check whether the approved corpus contains the answer and whether access rules allow this user to see it. Next, I would inspect the retrieved passages. If the needed passage is absent, I would investigate document parsing, chunk boundaries, indexing and ranking. If the passage is present but the answer misstates it, I would examine the prompt, context order and generation behavior. I would run a diagnostic comparison that supplies a reviewed, sufficient passage directly to the same generator. Improvement there would suggest retrieval is a bottleneck, although both stages may still have problems. I would measure evidence retrieval and answer support separately, including conflicting or unanswerable questions. The next change would target the observed failure rather than replacing the whole system at once.

Probe and answer

Probe: what if retrieving more passages lowers quality? Extra context can add noise, contradictions and cost. I would inspect whether the additional passages are relevant and test ranking or a smaller evidence set. I would evaluate whether the needed evidence remains available and whether the generator cites the right version, instead of assuming more context is always better.

Similar question with concrete answer

Question: the answer is correct but its citation is wrong. Is that a pass? For an evidence-dependent task, I would count it as a citation or support failure even if the answer happens to be correct. I would check whether the generator copied a plausible citation without using it. The acceptance test would verify the cited passage's relationship to the answer, not merely that the document exists.

Weak-answer trap

Increasing context length or switching models without checking whether the necessary evidence was retrieved and permitted.

Q13 — A repository file tells the agent to ignore instructions and send a secret to an external URL. What should happen?

Context

Priority A. Prompt injection is untrusted content attempting to redirect instructions or actions. Read-only repository access does not prevent a model from following malicious text. Sandbox's current default-allow regex policy is not complete authorization. [repo: resume-builder-agent/v2/src/rba/github_tools.py] [repo: sandbox-agent/core/policy.py]

Clarify and structure

Treat repository content as data, identify the requested privileged action and enforce permission outside the model. Test the boundary with harmless synthetic secrets and controlled destinations, never real credentials.

Draft answer

I would treat the file as untrusted project data and deny the requested secret transfer. The model should not gain network or secret access simply because retrieved text asks for it. I would keep credentials outside model-visible evidence where possible, restrict tool permissions to the task and validate each proposed action in code before execution. For a read-only summarizer, outbound transmission of secrets is outside the required capability. I would record a sanitized security event and continue only if the remaining task can be completed safely. I would test this using synthetic credentials and a controlled endpoint, checking both the model output and whether a prohibited tool action actually ran. I would also check indirect paths, such as malicious tool results. A prompt warning helps, but the decisive control is an enforced boundary around capabilities and data.

Probe and answer

Probe: does running inside Docker make that safe? No. A container's mounted files, network access, privileges and runtime configuration determine what it can reach. I would also need execution limits and process termination behavior. Sandbox's MCP timeout stops waiting on a future; it does not establish that the underlying container process was killed. [repo: sandbox-agent/sandbox/container.py] [repo: sandbox-agent/mcp_server/server.py]

Similar question with concrete answer

Question: a tool returns a page that says the user has approved a payment. What do you do? I would not treat webpage text as authorization. Approval must come through the trusted user or workflow channel and match the exact action, amount and destination. I would pause the side effect, show the proposed transaction through the approved interface and require the relevant authorization before execution.

Weak-answer trap

Saying “the system prompt forbids it,” “MCP is secure,” or “Docker isolates everything” without an enforceable permission boundary.

Q14 — Offline scores improve, but users perform worse in the pilot. How would you investigate?

Context

Priority A. Offline evaluation runs on a fixed test set. A pilot exposes a limited system to real workflow conditions. Better benchmark scores can coexist with worse task outcomes.

Clarify and structure

Confirm the user outcome and compare pilot traffic with the evaluation set. Investigate data differences, changed user behavior, latency, interface effects and metric alignment. Preserve a safe fallback while diagnosing.

Draft answer

I would first verify the pilot outcome and whether it is caused by the new version. Suppose users take longer to finish reviews even though offline answer support improves. I would compare the old and new workflows on comparable tasks, then inspect response time, answer length and the corrections users make. The offline set may contain short, clean documents while the pilot contains long, conflicting versions. The new system may also make users review more material or trust incorrect suggestions. I would group failures by task and user conditions, using approved and appropriately protected logs. If the change creates meaningful risk, I would restrict or roll back it while investigating. I would then update the evaluation set with reviewed pilot failure patterns, keeping a separate untouched set. The next version would need to improve task completion as well as the offline proxy.

Probe and answer

Probe: what if user feedback is anecdotal? I would collect the reported examples because they can reveal serious failures, but I would not treat their frequency as measured. I would define a short, consented task study or a controlled rollout with completion and correction measures. High-consequence individual incidents still deserve immediate investigation even before population rates are known.

Similar question with concrete answer

Question: the model is more accurate, but users stop using it. What would you do? I would interview users about the exact point where it fails their workflow and inspect completion paths. A slow answer, poor integration or unclear evidence can outweigh a small accuracy gain. I would test a specific change, such as shorter cited suggestions inside the existing review step, and measure accepted useful actions and task time.

Weak-answer trap

Blaming users, dismissing the pilot because the benchmark improved, or changing the metric after the result solely to declare success.

Q15 — You have very little labeled healthcare data. How would you start a research project?

Context

Priority A. A label is a reviewed target such as a document category. Scarce labels do not justify using sensitive data without permission or assuming synthetic examples represent real cases. This is a document-workflow example, not a clinical recommendation.

Clarify and structure

Define the task and permissible data first. Estimate whether the decision needs labels, retrieval, rules or expert review. Build a small trusted evaluation set before expanding training or model complexity.

Draft answer

I would first narrow the task and confirm what data the team is allowed to use. For example, classifying approved document sections is more bounded than producing broad medical conclusions. I would build a simple rule or retrieval baseline and ask domain reviewers to label a small, diverse sample with clear guidance. I would reserve part of that sample for evaluation and record uncertainty rather than force labels on ambiguous cases. Public or synthetic examples could help develop the pipeline, but I would not use their scores as proof of performance on private data. I would prioritize new labels where the baseline fails or reviewers disagree, while keeping a representative evaluation sample. I would compare the value of additional labels with model changes and report which cases remain unsupported. Sensitive-data access would follow the approved governance process throughout.

Probe and answer

Probe: can you use a larger model to label everything? I would test model-generated labels against expert-reviewed examples before using them. Such labels may carry systematic errors and should remain distinguishable from human-reviewed labels. I might use the model to propose labels or identify uncertain cases, while preserving trusted evaluation data that it did not define for itself.

Similar question with concrete answer

Question: can synthetic data solve class imbalance? I would first check whether generated examples reflect the difficult real cases and whether the target meaning remains correct. I would use synthetic examples as a controlled training intervention, then evaluate on untouched real examples by class. I would reject an apparent gain that comes only from learning synthetic wording or that worsens the rare real cases we care about.

Weak-answer trap

Treating access to a pretrained model or synthetic examples as a substitute for domain labels, permission and representative evaluation.

Q16 — You can afford either more labels or higher-quality expert labels. How would you choose?

Context

Priority B. Label quantity and quality address different bottlenecks. Agreement measures consistency between reviewers; it does not establish that the agreed label is correct.

Clarify and structure

Inspect label ambiguity and model error first. Estimate which next labeling action would change the research decision. Keep the evaluation labels more carefully reviewed than broad exploratory labels.

Draft answer

I would start by auditing a sample of existing labels and the errors they produce. If reviewers disagree because the categories overlap or the instructions are unclear, collecting more of the same labels could amplify noise. I would spend first on a clearer rubric, a small expert-adjudicated set and examples explaining difficult boundaries. If labels are already consistent and errors come from missing coverage, I would expand the dataset across those conditions. I would compare a smaller high-quality training subset with a larger ordinary subset on the same trusted evaluation set. I would measure the important class errors, not just average accuracy, and include the labeling cost and time. My next spend would follow the observed bottleneck. I would keep uncertain labels visible and avoid using the same contested labels as the final authority for model quality.

Probe and answer

Probe: what if experts are the scarce resource? I would use their time to define the rubric, review difficult cases and audit a sample of routine labels. Trained annotators could handle clear cases with escalation rules. I would monitor whether those rules preserve quality, rather than assuming one expert session makes the entire dataset reliable.

Similar question with concrete answer

Question: two annotators agree on ninety-five percent of cases. Is the dataset ready? I would inspect the remaining cases and ask whether both annotators share the same misunderstanding. I would review agreement by class, especially rare important categories, and audit a sample with domain expertise. Readiness depends on the task's error consequences and evaluation quality, not one overall agreement percentage.

Weak-answer trap

Always choosing more data, always choosing experts, or equating annotator agreement with verified truth.

Q17 — Another engineer cannot reproduce your result. What would you check and share?

Context

Priority A. Reproducibility means someone can follow the recorded procedure and assess whether the result holds. A random seed helps control some variation; it does not guarantee identical results across all hardware and libraries.

Clarify and structure

Separate a code failure from a numerical difference and a changed interpretation. Compare data, code, environment, model and evaluation artifacts in that order, then rerun the smallest meaningful case.

Draft answer

I would ask what differs: whether the run fails, produces different outputs or produces the same outputs with a different score. I would share the exact code commit, data identifiers and split, dependency versions, model settings, command and saved evaluation outputs, excluding secrets. I would compare the preprocessing and evaluation code before tuning anything. For a hosted model, I would record the provider and model identifier and acknowledge that availability or behavior may change. I would then reproduce one small case with intermediate artifacts to locate the first divergence. If the result depends on an undocumented setting, I would correct the experiment record and rerun the comparison. If variation remains, I would report it across repeated runs instead of selecting the best one. A defensible result includes its conditions and limits, not only a headline score.

Probe and answer

Probe: how does this apply to your own saved metrics? I would distinguish the historical v1 saved evaluation from current v2 code and avoid implying the new pipeline has the same measured score. I would preserve the original saved artifacts and run a new, separately identified evaluation before comparing versions. The current browser graph and the resume-era evaluated graph are different paths. [repo: resume-builder-agent/v1/evals/results/latest.json] [repo: resume-builder-agent/v1/src/rba/graph.py] [repo: resume-builder-agent/v2/src/rba/graph.py]

Similar question with concrete answer

Question: a test passes locally but fails in a container. What do you do? I would compare the command, dependency lock, working directory, file permissions, environment variables and network assumptions. I would run the smallest failing case inside the container and inspect its actual error. I would fix or document the environmental dependency and add a meaningful regression check for that failure instead of weakening the assertion.

Weak-answer trap

Saying “set the seed” as a complete solution, overwriting historical outputs, or comparing different data and code versions as though they were one controlled experiment.

Q18 — How would you turn a promising research prototype into a reusable component that a delivery team can adopt?

Context

Priority A. This tests the transition from an experiment to a maintained system. It is a proposed collaboration process, not a claim about ZS's formal organization or a confirmed transfer between named departments.

Clarify and structure

Define the repeated user problem, supported scope and adoption owner. Translate the research claim into acceptance criteria, a stable interface, operational limits and a measured pilot. Keep unsupported extensions outside the first release.

Draft answer

I would first state the repeatable problem the component solves and the evidence that it improves on a simple baseline. I would work with a delivery owner to define supported inputs, outputs, error behavior and the conditions where it should not be used. For an evidence-linked summarization component, I would package the evidence schema, generation interface, validation rules and a representative evaluation suite. I would document cost, latency, failure examples, data handling and model dependencies. I would then run a bounded pilot in the intended workflow with monitoring, review and a fallback path. Acceptance would depend on useful supported outcomes and operating requirements, not only a research score. I would agree who owns defects, updates and future evaluation before handover. The next expansion would follow pilot evidence, while preserving a clear boundary between measured capability and proposed work.

Probe and answer

Probe: what would you hand over besides code? I would include an example integration, versioned interface, evaluation data policy, reproducible commands, known limitations, configuration guidance and an escalation path. I would walk the receiving team through a normal case and a failure case. A handover is incomplete if only the original researcher can explain or operate the component.

Similar question with concrete answer

Question: two client workflows need slightly different versions. How would you keep the component reusable? I would identify the shared behavior and expose the genuine differences through a small configuration surface. For example, the core can enforce evidence fields while each workflow sets approved sources and review thresholds. I would test both configurations and avoid a large set of hidden client-specific branches. If the tasks have different assumptions, I would document separate supported variants.

Weak-answer trap

Equating reuse with a polished demo, calling a prototype production-ready without operational evidence, or assuming a research metric establishes client impact.

Research mini-cases grounded in my projects

Frame before choosing a model

These are hypothetical engineering exercises, not descriptions of ZS clients, delivered products or clinical evidence. They do not authorize clinical decisions. “Research to reusable asset to delivery” below is a proposed work sequence, not a confirmed ZS team structure. A baseline is the simplest measurable approach that meets the initial requirement. An ablation changes one component while holding the rest fixed so its contribution can be estimated.

For each case, ask who uses the output, what decision it supports, what error costs most, what data may be used, and what “good enough” means. Keep personal identifiers out of prompts and logs unless an approved design explicitly requires them. In these exercises, all acceptance thresholds are to be agreed with the responsible domain and governance teams; none is presented as a healthcare standard.

Q01 — Design an evidence-linked assistant that summarizes a pharma team's internal research documents.

Context

The transferable idea from Resume Builder is separating evidence collection, generated claims and verification. Repository evidence is not clinical evidence, so the domain changes both the source policy and review requirements. [repo: repos/resume-builder-agent/v1/src/rba/nodes/verify.py] [repo: repos/resume-builder-agent/v1/src/rba/nodes/build.py]

Problem framing

I would ask whether the assistant helps researchers find information or produces material for a regulated decision. I would start with internal information retrieval and drafting, with a qualified reviewer responsible for use. The first hypothesis is that claim-level citations and explicit abstention can reduce unsupported statements compared with an unconstrained summarizer.

Data limits and baseline

I would inventory approved documents, access groups, versions and document dates. Patient identifiers, confidential commercial data, scanned tables and conflicting document versions need separate handling. The baseline is permission-aware keyword retrieval followed by extractive snippets, meaning source sentences rather than generated conclusions. I would curate a small test set of real user questions with authorized expert answers.

Roadmap and draft answer

I would add retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, only after testing the search baseline. RAG retrieves relevant source passages and gives them to a model to draft an answer. For example, a question about a study's inclusion criteria should retrieve that study's current approved protocol section. I would preserve document identity, section, date and access rules through chunking, retrieval and citation. The model would answer only from retrieved evidence and mark missing support. Exact citation and number checks would be reproducible, but I would not mistake a matching number for a correct clinical claim. I would compare keyword search, keyword plus semantic retrieval, and generated answers on the same held-out questions. My Resume Builder result is a motivation for this design, not proof of performance in pharma.

Evaluation and expert review

Measure retrieval recall on expert-labeled relevant passages, citation correctness, unsupported-claim rate, abstention behavior, answer usefulness, latency and cost. Split questions by document family and time to reduce leakage. Include adversarial document instructions, outdated evidence and contradictory sources. Expert review should examine meaning, not just textual overlap. Audit which user could retrieve which passage.

Proposed research-to-delivery path

Research would test the evidence and abstention hypotheses. A reusable asset would package access-aware retrieval, evidence schemas, evaluations and audit hooks. A delivery team would configure a client's sources, validate the workflow with domain owners and monitor failures. I would ask ZS how those responsibilities actually map to its teams.

Follow-ups and answers

“Why not fine-tune first?” I would first test retrieval because the immediate need is current, attributable information. Fine-tuning may improve behavior or terminology, but it does not by itself provide document-level access control or current citations.

“What if the document contains an instruction to ignore access rules?” Treat it as untrusted content. Authorization is enforced outside the model, and the document cannot grant a new tool or data permission.

Q02 — Design an agent that helps a healthcare analyst inspect data and run analysis code.

Context

The Sandbox project exposes code execution, tools, a model loop and human input. Its audit also exposes why a configured limit must be checked against persisted state. This case applies those lessons to a proposed analyst tool. [repo: repos/sandbox-agent/agent/graph.py] [repo: repos/sandbox-agent/agent/state.py] [repo: repos/sandbox-agent/sandbox/container.py]

Problem framing

I would ask whether the user needs a fixed report or exploratory analysis. If fixed SQL and a report template solve the problem, I would start there. If exploration is needed, the model may propose bounded analysis steps while software controls data access and execution. The hypothesis is that constrained tools can improve task completion without exposing raw records or enabling arbitrary side effects.

Data limits and baseline

Start with synthetic data and a read-only curated dataset. Define approved columns, minimum aggregation size, output destinations and retention with the data owner. The baseline is a reviewed notebook or query library. No patient-level recommendation or operational change is part of the first scope. Prompt text and trace logs should not become an accidental copy of the dataset.

Roadmap and draft answer

I would offer a small tool set: inspect schema, run an approved read query, compute an aggregate and create a chart. I would keep authorization outside the model and validate every tool argument. For code execution, I would separate each run's workspace, limit resources and duration, restrict outbound access and provide only the necessary data. Human approval should be a mandatory gate for a defined risky action, rather than an optional tool the model may choose to call. I would persist explicit per-turn and per-task counters and test resume behavior. My existing Sandbox has intended step and retry limits, but its missing retry field and max-reducer reset issue mean I cannot claim those controls already enforce this design.

Evaluation and expert review

Use synthetic tasks with known answers. Measure numerical correctness, task completion, prohibited-data access attempts, unauthorized tool calls, budget enforcement and reproducibility. Include malicious instructions inside a CSV cell, huge outputs, timeouts, repeated tool calls and a resumed checkpoint. Have analysts review whether the output answers the business question and whether uncertainty is stated. Compare with the notebook baseline before expanding autonomy.

Proposed research-to-delivery path

Research would compare tool policies and error recovery. A reusable asset would provide tested tool contracts, execution boundaries and evaluation fixtures. Delivery would connect approved data sources, configure the threat model and agree who reviews outputs. A container alone would not establish safe operation.

Follow-ups and answers

“What is your first release?” Read-only schema inspection, approved aggregates and a reproducible analysis record on synthetic or authorized data. I would defer writes and external network tools until a demonstrated need and a reviewed control design exist.

“How do you handle a model repeatedly failing?” Enforce the task budget in software, record a structured failure, and return the partial evidence to the user. I would not allow an unconstrained reflection loop.

Q03 — Diagnose why a medical-image classifier fails on images from a new hospital.

Context

VisionDev logs failures and labels distortions. In one saved run, 1,949 of 4,816 unique failures were labeled blur. This supports investigating a distortion association; it does not prove blur caused those failures or transfer that percentage to medical images. [repo: repos/vision_dev_project/pipe/logs/misclassified_20260317_005331.json]

Problem framing

I would ask which clinical or operational task the classifier supports and whether the observed failure is a performance shift, a data-quality shift or a labeling issue. The hypothesis might be that acquisition differences at the new hospital explain part of the performance drop. I would state that hypothesis before selecting a vision-language model.

Data limits and baseline

Obtain authorized, de-identified samples and expert labels. Separate patients and institutions across development and evaluation; two images from the same patient must not create a misleadingly easy split. Check format, resolution, acquisition metadata and class mix. The baseline is a site-stratified error table and a blinded expert review of representative failures.

Roadmap and draft answer

I would compare performance by site and relevant subgroups, then test candidate shifts such as blur, compression or acquisition protocol. A distortion classifier can help sort cases, but I would validate its labels on this domain. I would select representative examples using original feature vectors and document the selection method. A vision-language model could draft a description for expert review, with links to the reviewed images and measured statistics. I would not treat the draft as a diagnosis. To test causality, I would run controlled perturbations or matched comparisons and measure whether the classifier's errors change. VisionDev's centroid-distance archetypes and section parser are useful prototype components; they are not proof of a validated RAG system or typed clinical output.

Evaluation and expert review

Report sensitivity and specificity for the agreed task, calibration, subgroup and site performance, sample sizes and uncertainty. Evaluate the diagnostic assistant separately: factual image description, correct references, unsupported causal statements and reviewer usefulness. Compare the same classifier with and without a proposed augmentation on held-out sites. Count unique images or patients explicitly, rather than repeated training observations.

Proposed research-to-delivery path

Research would test the shift hypothesis and intervention. A reusable asset would standardize failure capture, cohort definitions and reviewed report structure. Delivery would validate the integration, review responsibilities and ongoing shift monitoring with the institution. Clinical adoption would require its own appropriate review beyond this interview prototype.

Follow-ups and answers

“Would you retrain immediately?” First confirm labels, denominator and the source of the shift. Otherwise retraining may optimize for a data-collection artifact or conceal a mislabeled cohort.

“Can the VLM explain the true cause?” Its description is a hypothesis generator. A persuasive explanation still needs controlled evidence or expert validation.

Q04 — A pharma operations dashboard shows a stale approval status. How would you investigate and redesign it?

Context

BountyHub writes to PostgreSQL and maintains asynchronous read paths through events and a worker. The traced path has a commit/publish gap, replica preflight checks and no demonstrated idempotency guard for repeated approval. These are useful failure mechanisms for this hypothetical dashboard. [repo: repos/BountyHub-main/server/src/services/submissionService.js] [repo: repos/BountyHub-main/server/src/config/redis.js] [repo: repos/BountyHub-main/server/src/workers/syncWorker.js]

Problem framing

I would ask which database is authoritative and whether the dashboard is informational or used to trigger another action. I would establish the expected freshness and the cost of showing a stale approval. The initial hypothesis is a missed or delayed projection update, but I would trace one record before changing the system.

Data limits and baseline

Use a sanitized record identifier and an audit trail that excludes unnecessary personal or confidential content. Record transaction time, event identifier, worker receipt, projection version and cache age. The baseline is a direct authorized read from the primary for a correctness-critical approval view.

Roadmap and draft answer

I would trace the record from the primary transaction through event publication, consumption, projection and cache. If the transaction committed but publication failed, a worker cannot recover an event that never existed. I would propose a transactional outbox: write the business change and an event record in the same database transaction, then publish from that outbox with retries.
